title: feat(mp): add ARC eviction policy
body:
## What this PR does Adds Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) to the multiprocess eviction framework. - `ARCEvictionPolicy` implements the distributed `EvictionPolicy` contract used by MP L1 and L2 eviction controllers. - L1 can select it with `--eviction-policy ARC`. - Each L2 adapter can select it independently with `"eviction": {"eviction_policy": "ARC"}`. ## Design ARC maintains four ordered key indexes: - `T1`: resident keys seen recently. - `T2`: resident keys seen repeatedly. - `B1`: key-only history for completed policy evictions from `T1`. - `B2`: key-only history for completed policy evictions from `T2`. A key recreated from `B1` increases the target size `p` of `T1`; a key recreated from `B2` decreases it. This lets the policy adapt between recency-heavy and frequency-heavy workloads. Ghost lists contain only `ObjectKey` metadata, not KV data. The implementation follows MP lifecycle callbacks: writes create or update policy entries, accesses promote entries, and confirmed removals retire policy-selected victims into ghost history. A selected key remains resident until the L1 manager or L2 adapter reports that deletion completed. Other lifecycle removals are forgotten without creating ARC feedback. The original ARC paper's `REPLACE(x)` operation can use the incoming key when breaking a tie at the adaptive boundary. MP eviction runs later in an independent pressure loop, so there is no corresponding `x`. Following vLLM's CPU-offload ARC variant, this policy uses the request-independent rule `len(T1) >= int(p)` to select from `T1`; otherwise it selects from `T2`. The MP eviction interface supplies a pressure ratio rather than a fixed entry capacity, so the policy uses the largest observed resident-key count to bound ghost history and `p`. This is an entry-based policy and is the closest fit for fixed-size KV chunks and fixed-slot adapters; it is not byte-weighted for variable-sized objects. ARC is a global policy and does not provide per-`cache_salt` isolation. Deployments that need quota-driven isolation should continue to use `IsolatedLRU`. ## Validation - `pytest -q tests/v1/distributed/test_arc_eviction_policy.py tests/v1/distributed/test_lru_eviction_policy.py tests/v1/distributed/test_isolated_lru_eviction_policy.py` — 55 passed. - `SKIP=rust-fmt,rust-clippy pre-commit run --all-files` — passed; Rust hooks were skipped because no Rust files changed. - `make -C docs clean html SPHINXOPTS=-q` — succeeded; existing repository warnings remain. The tests cover ARC ordering, floating-point adaptation through `B1`/`B2`, the `T1 == int(p)` boundary, eligibility filtering, incomplete deletions, explicit removals, L1/L2 configuration, and both MP listener bridges. ## MP end-to-end validation An A\/B validation was run of LRU and ARC against PR head `6c961db763877f6efc1be47e2af8657ecb5111fa`. Each arm used a fresh LMCache MP server and the same vLLM configuration and request sequence; only `--eviction-policy` changed. ### Environment - Host: x86_64 Linux 5.15, 2 x Intel Xeon Platinum 8460Y+ (80 physical cores / 160 logical CPUs) - Python 3.12 - vLLM: `0.1.dev19657+g163ae96f1` - LMCache: this PR at `6c961db7` - Model: DeepSeek-V2-Lite, BF16, tensor parallel size 2 - Connector: `LMCacheMPConnector`, `lmcache_driven` transfer mode, separate LMCache MP server - vLLM prefix caching disabled, so the measured external hits come from LMCache rather than vLLM APC - LMCache L1: 0.09375 GiB, 256-token chunks, 2 workers, 80% eviction watermark, 25% eviction ratio - Sequential requests with `temperature=0` and `max_tokens=1` The relevant service configuration was: ```bash python -m lmcache.cli.main server \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 6655 --http-port 18180 \ --supported-transfer-mode lmcache_driven \ --l1-size-gb 0.09375 --chunk-size 256 --max-workers 2 \ --eviction-policy LRU \ --eviction-trigger-watermark 0.80 --eviction-ratio 0.25 ``` The ARC arm used exactly the same command with `--eviction-policy ARC`. vLLM was started with: ```bash python -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main serve /path/to/DeepSeek-V2-Lite \ --served-model-name DeepSeek-V2-Lite \ --dtype bfloat16 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --max-model-len 1280 --block-size 16 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching --no-enable-chunked-prefill \ --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_module_path":"lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_connector","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"127.0.0.1","lmcache.mp.port":6655,"lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode":"lmcache_driven"}}' ``` ### Workload This test targets ARC's scan-resistance behavior: 1. Send a 32-token warm-up request (smaller than one LMCache chunk). 2. Prime two independent 512-token hot prefixes (four chunks total). 3. Access both hot prefixes two more times, for three accesses per hot prefix before the scan. This promotes the resident hot entries into ARC's frequent set. 4. Scan six one-time 512-token cold prefixes (12 new chunks), pausing 1.1 seconds between requests so the 1 Hz eviction loop can run. 5. Wait four seconds for pending pressure-driven evictions to finish, then snapshot LMCache `/metrics`. 6. Probe the two original hot prefixes once each and compute the metric delta. 7. Verify that every probe completion exactly matches its deterministic prime completion. The hot working set is deliberately smaller than L1, while the combined hot plus cold working set exceeds it. This makes LRU evict the oldest hot entries during the scan, while ARC should retain repeatedly accessed entries and evict scan entries instead. ### Results | Metric | LRU | ARC | Interpretation | |---|---:|---:|---| | Cold-scan mean request latency | 324.9 ms | 322.2 ms | Comparable scan cost | | Evicted chunks before hot probe | 7 | 7 | Identical eviction pressure | | Triggered eviction loops before hot probe | 3 | 3 | Identical pressure-loop activity | | Allocation / read failures before hot probe | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | Clean comparison before probing | | Hot-probe hit tokens | 0 / 1024 | 1024 / 1024 | ARC retained all hot-prefix tokens | | Hot-probe token hit rate | 0% | 100% | +100 percentage points | | Hot-probe mean request latency | 310.0 ms | 111.7 ms | **64.0% lower; 2.77x speedup** | | Probe outputs match prime outputs | Yes | Yes | Deterministic correctness preserved | Per-request hot-probe latencies were 325.5/294.5 ms with LRU and 116.7/106.7 ms with ARC. The LRU misses also attempted to write the recomputed chunks back and recorded two allocation failures during the probe; ARC performed no probe-time writes or allocations because both prefixes hit. There were no allocation or read failures in either arm before the probe. ### Conclusion and scope This end-to-end result validates the intended MP integration and demonstrates the expected benefit for a hot-set-plus-cold-scan workload: under the same physical L1 capacity, number of evictions, and eviction-loop activity, LRU lost the hot prefixes while ARC retained all of them. In this scenario, that changed the LMCache hit rate from 0% to 100% and reduced mean hot-prefix request latency by 64.0%. This is a focused CPU functional/performance A/B with one run and two hot-prefix probes. It demonstrates the policy behavior and benefit direction, but it is not a production GPU throughput or tail-latency claim. A larger GPU evaluation should add concurrent traffic, repeated trials, and P50/P95/P99 TTFT and throughput measurements. ### When ARC is a good fit ARC is most useful when the MP cache sees both reuse and scan pollution, for example: - A repeatedly reused set of system prompts, shared conversation prefixes, RAG documents, or agent/tool prefixes is mixed with a stream of one-time prefixes. - Batch or indexing traffic periodically scans a working set larger than L1 and would evict interactive hot prefixes under LRU. - The balance between recently introduced prefixes and repeatedly reused prefixes changes over time. ARC can adapt that balance through ghost-history feedback instead of using a fixed recency/frequency split. ARC is unlikely to provide a meaningful benefit when nearly every prefix is used only once, when the complete hot working set already fits comfortably in L1, or when the workload is already well served by pure recency. In those cases it adds policy metadata without creating additional cache hits. There are also two current implementation boundaries: - This ARC implementation is global and ignores `cache_salt`. Deployments that require strict per-tenant/quota isolation should use `IsolatedLRU` rather than ARC. - Its learned capacity is entry-count based rather than byte-weighted. It matches fixed-size KV chunks and fixed-slot adapters best; workloads with materially different object sizes need additional validation. ### Recommended starting configuration `p` is not a user-facing configuration value. It starts at zero and is adjusted automatically: reinsertion from B1 increases the target recent-set size, while reinsertion from B2 decreases it and gives more space to the frequent set. Operators should size the physical cache and tune pressure behavior instead. A reasonable production starting point is the existing default pressure configuration: ```bash --eviction-policy ARC \ --eviction-trigger-watermark 0.80 \ --eviction-ratio 0.20 ``` Practical tuning guidance: - Size `--l1-size-gb` so the expected hot working set normally consumes no more than roughly 50-70% of L1, leaving scan/burst headroom before the 80% watermark. If the hot set itself is near or above the watermark, ARC cannot protect it indefinitely. - Keep the 0.80 watermark and 0.20 ratio first; do not copy this small-cache test's 0.25 ratio blindly into production. - If burst traffic causes `lmcache_mp_l1_allocation_failure_chunks_total` to increase before the 1 Hz eviction loop catches up, increase L1 capacity first. If capacity cannot be increased, trigger earlier (about 0.70-0.75) and/or evict a larger batch (about 0.25-0.30). - If allocation failures remain zero but eviction is unnecessarily aggressive, try a higher watermark (about 0.85-0.90) or a smaller batch (about 0.10-0.15), and verify that tail latency does not regress. - Keep the existing known-good chunk size initially. Smaller chunks provide finer partial-prefix reuse and eviction granularity but increase key metadata and operation count; chunk size is a general cache-layout trade-off, not an ARC-specific knob. For rollout, compare ARC against LRU with the same L1 size and production request trace. Allow enough warm-up time for B1/B2 feedback, then evaluate delta token hit rate, P50/P95/P99 TTFT, throughput, evicted chunks, triggered eviction loops, and allocation/read failures. Enable ARC when it improves repeated-prefix hit rate and tail latency under scan pressure without introducing allocation failures; the focused test above is evidence for that workload shape, not a universal default recommendation. ## Reproduction scripts The end-to-end report included the service commands and workload description but omitted the complete request generator and metrics collector. The full scripts are included below. The Bash driver is a path-parameterized version of the script used for the reported run. The only changes are replacing the fixed container model/output paths with environment variables and adding configurable ports; the LMCache/vLLM arguments and workload are unchanged. Prerequisites: 1. Check out this PR at `6c961db763877f6efc1be47e2af8657ecb5111fa` and build/install its CPU native extensions. 2. Use a CPU-enabled vLLM environment where `python -m lmcache.cli.main` and `python -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main` resolve to the intended checkouts. When running directly from source, set `PYTHONPATH` accordingly. 3. Download DeepSeek-V2-Lite locally. 4. Save the two code blocks below as `reproduce_arc_e2e_arm.sh` and `arc_e2e_hot_scan.py` in the same directory. 5. Run each policy with a fresh service pair: ```bash chmod +x reproduce_arc_e2e_arm.sh arc_e2e_hot_scan.py MODEL_PATH=/path/to/DeepSeek-V2-Lite ./reproduce_arc_e2e_arm.sh LRU MODEL_PATH=/path/to/DeepSeek-V2-Lite ./reproduce_arc_e2e_arm.sh ARC ``` The raw results will be written to `arc-e2e-output/results/LRU.json` and `arc-e2e-output/results/ARC.json`. The driver terminates its LMCache and vLLM process groups after each arm, so the two policies do not share cache state.
reproduce_arc_e2e_arm.sh ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail policy=${1:?usage: MODEL_PATH=/path/to/model $0 LRU|ARC} case "$policy" in LRU|ARC) ;; *) echo "invalid policy: $policy" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac : "${MODEL_PATH:?set MODEL_PATH to the local DeepSeek-V2-Lite directory}" MODEL_NAME=${MODEL_NAME:-DeepSeek-V2-Lite} PYTHON_BIN=${PYTHON_BIN:-python} LMCACHE_PORT=${LMCACHE_PORT:-6655} LMCACHE_HTTP_PORT=${LMCACHE_HTTP_PORT:-18180} VLLM_PORT=${VLLM_PORT:-8034} OUTPUT_ROOT=${OUTPUT_ROOT:-$PWD/arc-e2e-output} SCRIPT_DIR=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd) CLIENT_SCRIPT=${CLIENT_SCRIPT:-$SCRIPT_DIR/arc_e2e_hot_scan.py} export PYTHONHASHSEED=0 export LMCACHE_DISABLE_BANNER=1 export LMCACHE_LOG_LEVEL=INFO export VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu export VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE=4 mkdir -p "$OUTPUT_ROOT/logs" "$OUTPUT_ROOT/results" lmcache_log="$OUTPUT_ROOT/logs/lmcache_${policy}.log" vllm_log="$OUTPUT_ROOT/logs/vllm_${policy}.log" lmcache_pid= vllm_pid= cleanup() { if [[ -n "$vllm_pid" ]]; then kill -TERM -- "-$vllm_pid" 2>/dev/null || true fi if [[ -n "$lmcache_pid" ]]; then kill -TERM -- "-$lmcache_pid" 2>/dev/null || true fi sleep 5 if [[ -n "$vllm_pid" ]]; then kill -KILL -- "-$vllm_pid" 2>/dev/null || true fi if [[ -n "$lmcache_pid" ]]; then kill -KILL -- "-$lmcache_pid" 2>/dev/null || true fi } trap cleanup EXIT setsid "$PYTHON_BIN" -m lmcache.cli.main server \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port "$LMCACHE_PORT" --http-port "$LMCACHE_HTTP_PORT" \ --supported-transfer-mode lmcache_driven \ --l1-size-gb 0.09375 --chunk-size 256 --max-workers 2 \ --eviction-policy "$policy" \ --eviction-trigger-watermark 0.80 --eviction-ratio 0.25 \ --enable-extra-logging --extra-logging-interval 1 \ >"$lmcache_log" 2>&1 & lmcache_pid=$! for _ in $(seq 1 60); do if curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:${LMCACHE_HTTP_PORT}/healthcheck" >/dev/null 2>&1; then break fi if ! kill -0 "$lmcache_pid" 2>/dev/null; then tail -200 "$lmcache_log" >&2 exit 1 fi sleep 2 done curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:${LMCACHE_HTTP_PORT}/healthcheck" >/dev/null kv_config=$(printf '%s' \ "{\"kv_connector\":\"LMCacheMPConnector\",\"kv_role\":\"kv_both\"," \ "\"kv_connector_module_path\":\"lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_connector\"," \ "\"kv_connector_extra_config\":{\"lmcache.mp.host\":\"127.0.0.1\"," \ "\"lmcache.mp.port\":${LMCACHE_PORT},\"lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode\":\"lmcache_driven\"}}") setsid "$PYTHON_BIN" -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main serve "$MODEL_PATH" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_NAME" \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port "$VLLM_PORT" \ --dtype bfloat16 --trust-remote-code \ --tensor-parallel-size 2 --max-model-len 1280 --block-size 16 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching --no-enable-chunked-prefill \ --kv-transfer-config "$kv_config" \ >"$vllm_log" 2>&1 & vllm_pid=$! for _ in $(seq 1 180); do if curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:${VLLM_PORT}/health" >/dev/null 2>&1; then break fi if ! kill -0 "$vllm_pid" 2>/dev/null; then tail -200 "$vllm_log" >&2 exit 1 fi sleep 2 done curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:${VLLM_PORT}/health" >/dev/null "$PYTHON_BIN" "$CLIENT_SCRIPT" \ --policy "$policy" \ --engine-url "http://127.0.0.1:${VLLM_PORT}" \ --metrics-url "http://127.0.0.1:${LMCACHE_HTTP_PORT}/metrics" \ --model "$MODEL_NAME" \ --output "$OUTPUT_ROOT/results/${policy}.json" ```
arc_e2e_hot_scan.py ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Run a deterministic hot-set / cold-scan LMCache MP benchmark.""" from __future__ import annotations import argparse import json import math import statistics import time import urllib.request from pathlib import Path from typing import Any METRICS = ( "lmcache_mp_lookup_requested_tokens_total", "lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_tokens_total", "lmcache_mp_l1_evicted_chunks_total", "lmcache_mp_l1_eviction_loop_triggered_total", "lmcache_mp_l1_allocation_failure_chunks_total", "lmcache_mp_l1_read_failure_chunks_total", "lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total", ) def percentile(values: list[float], p: float) -> float: if not values: return 0.0 ordered = sorted(values) return ordered[max(0, math.ceil(p * len(ordered)) - 1)] def fetch_metrics(url: str) -> dict[str, float]: with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as response: body = response.read().decode("utf-8") totals = {name: 0.0 for name in METRICS} for raw in body.splitlines(): if not raw or raw.startswith("#"): continue metric, _, value = raw.partition(" ") base = metric.split("{", 1)[0] if base in totals: totals[base] += float(value) return totals def metric_delta(after: dict[str, float], before: dict[str, float]) -> dict[str, float]: return {name: after.get(name, 0.0) - before.get(name, 0.0) for name in METRICS} def make_prompt(doc_id: int, length: int) -> list[int]: # DeepSeek-V2-Lite has a large vocabulary. The first tokens make every # document's first chunk unique; chained hashes then make all later chunks # unique too. The remainder stays identical to keep compute comparable. header = [1000 + doc_id % 10000, 12000 + doc_id % 10000, 200, 201] filler = [3456, 4567, 5678, 6789] prompt = header + (filler * math.ceil((length - len(header)) / len(filler))) return prompt[:length] def request_completion(endpoint: str, model: str, prompt: list[int]) -> dict[str, Any]: payload = json.dumps( { "model": model, "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0, } ).encode("utf-8") request = urllib.request.Request( endpoint, data=payload, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, method="POST", ) start = time.perf_counter() with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=600) as response: result = json.loads(response.read()) latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000 return { "latency_ms": latency_ms, "text": result["choices"][0]["text"], "usage": result.get("usage", {}), } def summarize(samples: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, float]: values = [float(sample["latency_ms"]) for sample in samples] return { "count": len(values), "mean_ms": statistics.fmean(values) if values else 0.0, "median_ms": statistics.median(values) if values else 0.0, "p90_ms": percentile(values, 0.90), "max_ms": max(values, default=0.0), } def main() -> None: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser() parser.add_argument("--policy", required=True, choices=("LRU", "ARC")) parser.add_argument("--engine-url", default="http://127.0.0.1:8034") parser.add_argument("--metrics-url", default="http://127.0.0.1:18180/metrics") parser.add_argument("--model", default="DeepSeek-V2-Lite") parser.add_argument("--prompt-length", type=int, default=512) parser.add_argument("--hot-count", type=int, default=2) parser.add_argument("--scan-count", type=int, default=6) parser.add_argument("--scan-pause-seconds", type=float, default=1.1) parser.add_argument("--output", type=Path, required=True) args = parser.parse_args() endpoint = args.engine_url.rstrip("/") + "/v1/completions" phases: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]] = { "hot_prime": [], "hot_promote": [], "cold_scan": [], "hot_probe": [], } expected_outputs: dict[int, str] = {} # Sub-chunk warmup: initializes model and connector without adding an # LMCache chunk. request_completion(endpoint, args.model, make_prompt(9999, 32)) for doc_id in range(args.hot_count): result = request_completion( endpoint, args.model, make_prompt(doc_id, args.prompt_length) ) phases["hot_prime"].append({"doc_id": doc_id, **result}) expected_outputs[doc_id] = result["text"] time.sleep(2) for _ in range(2): for doc_id in range(args.hot_count): result = request_completion( endpoint, args.model, make_prompt(doc_id, args.prompt_length) ) phases["hot_promote"].append({"doc_id": doc_id, **result}) time.sleep(2) for offset in range(args.scan_count): doc_id = 1000 + offset result = request_completion( endpoint, args.model, make_prompt(doc_id, args.prompt_length) ) phases["cold_scan"].append({"doc_id": doc_id, **result}) time.sleep(args.scan_pause_seconds) # Give the 1 Hz pressure loop multiple opportunities to finish deletions. time.sleep(4) metrics_before_probe = fetch_metrics(args.metrics_url) for doc_id in range(args.hot_count): result = request_completion( endpoint, args.model, make_prompt(doc_id, args.prompt_length) ) result["output_matches_prime"] = result["text"] == expected_outputs[doc_id] phases["hot_probe"].append({"doc_id": doc_id, **result}) time.sleep(2) metrics_after_probe = fetch_metrics(args.metrics_url) probe_delta = metric_delta(metrics_after_probe, metrics_before_probe) requested = probe_delta["lmcache_mp_lookup_requested_tokens_total"] hit = probe_delta["lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_tokens_total"] result = { "policy": args.policy, "scenario": { "prompt_length": args.prompt_length, "hot_count": args.hot_count, "hot_accesses_before_scan": 3, "scan_count": args.scan_count, }, "phase_summaries": {name: summarize(samples) for name, samples in phases.items()}, "phases": phases, "metrics_before_probe": metrics_before_probe, "metrics_after_probe": metrics_after_probe, "probe_metric_delta": probe_delta, "probe_token_hit_rate": hit / requested if requested else 0.0, "probe_outputs_match_prime": all( sample["output_matches_prime"] for sample in phases["hot_probe"] ), } args.output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) args.output.write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2), encoding="utf-8") print(json.dumps(result, indent=2)) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ```
## Checklist - [x] User-facing MP configuration and design documentation updated. - [x] Unit and MP lifecycle tests added. - [x] Every commit includes `Signed-off-by`. AI assistance (Codex) was used. The implementation and MP lifecycle paths were manually reviewed.

title: fix(mp): snapshot token IDs at session boundary
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/4916/files) against `dev`.

## Summary

- snapshot caller-provided token lists when updating a multiprocess `Session`
- prevent mutations performed outside the session lock from changing session state
- add a regression test that mutates the original list after `set_tokens()`

## Problem

`Session.set_tokens()` stored the caller-owned list by reference. A caller could mutate that list after the method returned, changing `session.token_ids` without acquiring the session lock. This also risks making the visible token sequence disagree with hashes cached by the session.

## Validation

Test-first reproduction before the fix:

```text
assert [999, 2, 3, 4] == [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

After the fix:

```text
python3 -m pytest -q tests/v1/multiprocess/test_session.py
28 passed, 84 warnings in 1.34s
```

Repository hooks:

```text
uv tool run pre-commit run --files lmcache/v1/multiprocess/session.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_session.py
All applicable hooks passed (SPDX, device checks, isort, ruff, ruff-format, codespell, mypy).
```

No performance benchmark is claimed: the intentional ownership boundary adds one O(n) list snapshot per `set_tokens()` call. This patch does not change the existing rolling-hash invalidation policy.

## Final-head reproducible integration log

Validated from an isolated worktree at exact commit `c9ab361b637cc34375243b9ce9043a7d5881f9ed` on macOS arm64 / Python 3.12.13 with the locally built LMCache native extensions:


```text
28 passed, 82 warnings in 1.16s
```

The verbose raw pytest log contains 190 lines and has SHA-256 `eb84073195776b3f6c8fc8fade5f211fa0f4ffe04028c41dc8fa4af691cc5b01`. title: [SDK] Add generation-fenced drop lifecycle
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/4900/files) against `dev`.

## Summary

- add a thread-safe, model-agnostic SDK lifecycle for asynchronous decode-time cache edits
- identify every edit by `(request_id, request_generation, operation_id, drop_round, source_kv_revision)`
- fence topology, policy, source-KV revision, and accepted sequence length; mismatches fail closed to recomputation
- make remote completion, local visibility, and plan consumption distinct, with exactly-once effect application
- keep abort/failure/stale paths idempotent, expose immutable metrics/snapshots, and bound old-generation diagnostic tombstones

This is the generic lifecycle/fencing layer from the token-dropping roadmap. It does not implement or change token-scoring policy. It complements the concrete vLLM MP abort fix in #4136 and the Q-across-decode work in #4527 rather than duplicating either change. Refs #4185.

## Correctness coverage

The 20 new CPU test cases cover:

- normal state progression and the separate source-reuse/local-visibility boundaries
- repeated and concurrent duplicate completion (exactly one remote record and one local application)
- repeated abort and late completion after abort, including malformed late metadata
- request-ID reuse across generations and delayed old-generation completion
- topology, policy, source-KV-revision, and accepted-sequence-length mismatch
- out-of-order completion/visibility, failure, invalid local transitions, and bounded tombstone pruning

## Validation

- `python -m pytest -q tests/sdk`: **56 passed, 1 skipped**
- full repository `pre-commit` on changed files: **passed** (SPDX, device-API bans, timeout ban, isort, Ruff, Ruff format, codespell, mypy)
- Python 3.12.13 CPU-only editable build with `NO_GPU_EXT=1`

Control-plane microbenchmark on Apple M5 / macOS 26.6.1, Python 3.12.13, seven repetitions:

- complete lifecycle (begin + four local phases + remote completion + local visibility + consume): median **7.768 us/op**, **128,730 ops/s** over 20,000 operations per repetition
- duplicate remote-completion no-op: median **1.451 us/event**, **688,961 events/s** over 200,000 events per repetition

These are absolute local CPU measurements, not a cross-machine performance claim.

## InfraSWE pre-PR check

- InfraSWE revision `191b9099f6d634b65998dac5604aeefc433673e7`
- InfraSWE suite: **283 passed**
- explicit LMCache `D1-target-bound` Draft validated and resolved as `source=local`, `target=explicit`
- candidate content digest: `sha256:d10e1f57dfb7ad72a360ffe140e1af1501430f91a7e91b75898e894241d3baa6`

The Draft is intentionally unsealed, so this check does **not** claim an official ProjectFit score or mergeability decision.

## Runnable L20 end-to-end notebook

Reviewer-runnable artifact: [`examples/token_dropping/generation_fenced_token_dropping.ipynb`](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/c179a4505b0d0748d1909133caa2cafe10ebb368/examples/token_dropping/generation_fenced_token_dropping.ipynb).

The first notebook cell contains the LMCache and vLLM startup commands. After both health checks pass, open the notebook and **Run All** from either the repository root or `examples/token_dropping`. Online installs need no model override. For an offline snapshot, set `HF_MODEL_NAME` and `LMCACHE_MODEL_NAME` to the same local snapshot path while leaving `VLLM_SERVED_MODEL_NAME` as the API alias; the notebook explains why these names differ.

Reproduced on NVIDIA L20; vLLM 0.25.1; PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130; CUDA 13.0; Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B; LMCacheMPConnector; 256-token chunks.

title: [SDK] Add topology-aware token selection plans
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/4901/files) against `dev`.

## Summary

- add deterministic `CacheTopologyDescriptor` and `TokenSelectionPlan` SDK types
- keep semantic retention decisions independent of model names, page tables, padded strides, and rank-local addresses
- validate request generation, decode round, accepted length, source-KV revision, topology fingerprint, policy revision, group identity, and selection lifetime before expansion
- require hybrid sibling families to be complete, non-overlapping equivalence sets rather than merely pairwise-symmetric fragments
- give all selection content a total canonical order so malformed duplicate selections produce an order-independent digest before fail-closed validation
- map dense, compressed, and sliding-window logical spans to full-block physical entry/byte ranges
- surface partial compressed blocks as explicit residual spans instead of silently widening destructive operations

`expand_plan()` is fail closed: any validation issue yields no physical operations and `validation.recompute_required == True`.

This PR intentionally does not add a scoring algorithm or model-specific DeepSeek logic. It provides an independent topology/plan foundation for Q-across-decode work such as #4527 and follows the SDK direction established by #3820. It is also independent of #4900, although their revision fields are designed to compose.

## Correctness coverage

The 30 focused CPU cases cover:

- Dense 256 logical -> 256 physical
- C4 256 logical -> 64 physical
- C128 256 logical -> 2 physical
- strict sliding-window boundaries
- partial compressed spans and residual-only sub-block spans
- complete, missing, internally inconsistent, overlapping, and incomplete hybrid families
- every live request/revision fence and accepted-token boundary
- unknown/duplicate groups, expired plans, and explicit recompute
- symmetric topology graphs, geometry/alignment invariants, stable content digests, and tamper rejection
- order-independent digests for malformed duplicate selections

The residual-only case caught and prevented a negative physical range during development; the final regression asserts an empty `start == end` physical range with the full logical span retained as residual work.

## Validation

Candidate `edd06a8604c1aec212642605c007efd5a64afe65` is rebased on `dev` at `86483cd63a544a0b52c51c0b139f39fa02be03d3`.

- `python -m pytest -q tests/sdk`: **66 passed, 1 skipped**
- targeted topology/plan suite: **30 passed**
- changed-file `pre-commit`: **passed** (SPDX, device-API bans, timeout ban, isort, Ruff, Ruff format, codespell, mypy; Rust hook skipped on macOS)
- `git diff --check`: **passed**
- DCO: **passed**
- Buildkite `k3-unit-tests`: **passed** ([build #8607](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-unit-tests/builds/8607), 21m40s)

The wider macOS test collection requires optional Triton and vLLM packages that are not installed locally; those modules fail during import before reaching this change. The focused SDK suite and project CI are the relevant executable gates.

## Control-plane benchmark

Apple M5 / macOS 26.6.1 / Python 3.12.13, seven independent fresh-process repetitions:

- two-group hybrid validation + physical expansion, 20,000 iterations/repetition: median **6.240 us/op** (range **5.975-6.609 us/op**), median **160,249 ops/s**
- incomplete-family fail-closed validation, 50,000 iterations/repetition: median **2.428 us/op** (range **2.271-2.563 us/op**), median **411,916 ops/s**

title: fix(mp/shm): fence unlink ownership across fork
body:
**Incremental review:** [Files changed](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/4917/files) against `dev`.

## Summary

- reset the inherited POSIX-SHM registry lock in forked children
- clear parent-owned unlink leases after fork without discarding inherited mappings
- verify that parent segments survive child exit while child-created segments are still cleaned

## Problem

The process-global `_OWNED_NAMES` registry is copied by `fork()`. A child that exits normally therefore runs the inherited atexit cleanup and unlinks segments that are still owned and used by its parent. The registry lock can also be inherited in a locked state if another parent thread held it at fork time.

## Fix

Register an `after_in_child` fork callback that installs a fresh registry lock and drops inherited unlink ownership. The address-to-mmap registry remains available so the child can close its own inherited mappings during shutdown. Any segment created after the fork is added normally and remains owned by the child.

## Validation

Test-first failure on the unmodified implementation:

```text
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: /lmc_pshm_fork_...
```

After the fix:

```text
uv run pytest -q tests/v1/multiprocess/test_posix_shm.py
5 passed, 80 warnings in 2.09s
```

The regression test also confirms that a segment created by the forked child is unlinked on child exit.

Repository hooks:

```text
uv tool run pre-commit run --files lmcache/v1/multiprocess/posix_shm.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_posix_shm.py
All applicable hooks passed (SPDX, device checks, isort, ruff, ruff-format, codespell, mypy).
```

No performance benchmark is claimed; the callback runs once per fork and performs constant-time lock replacement plus clearing the child-private ownership set.

<!-- final-head-e2e-log:start -->
## Final-head reproducible integration log

Validated from an isolated worktree at exact commit `c10ee4075cb2377dd6cef5b0d715a82fb8b5fff1` on macOS arm64 / Python 3.12.13 with the locally built LMCache native extensions:

```bash
python -m pytest -q tests/v1/multiprocess/test_posix_shm.py
```

```text
5 passed, 80 warnings in 3.26s
```

The verbose raw pytest log contains 19 lines and has SHA-256 `18777a8ce30bc633243676ce64857d5ee552e382a4c990557376835061bc6754`. The command above is the reviewer-runnable reproduction entry point and exercises the same checked-in tests and candidate code. This is a CPU control-plane/integration change, so a GPU notebook would add an indirect wrapper without increasing coverage; GPU/benchmark PRs carry Run-All notebooks separately.

title: [Bugfix][Test] Poll the MultiConnector peer mock through get_transfer_results
body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

`tests/v1/test_mp_connector_kv_roles.py::test_multi_connector_child_role_and_completion`
currently fails on `dev` for both `peer_delays_free=True` parametrizations
(`kv_both` and `kv_consumer`) with `assert set() == {'request'}`, which red-lines
the whole `test: 3.10 - 3.13` matrix on every PR.

vLLM's `MultiConnector` polls its children through `get_transfer_results()`, and
`KVConnectorBase_V1.get_transfer_results()` wraps `get_finished()`. Real
connectors such as `LMCacheMPConnector` therefore keep working while only
implementing `get_finished`. The peer in this test, however, is a bare
`MagicMock`: `get_transfer_results()` answers with another mock whose result
sets iterate empty, so the peer's completions are silently dropped and the
`get_finished.side_effect` sequence is never consumed.

This is an external regression, not an LMCache change: vLLM 0.29.0 (2026-09-09)
had `MultiConnector` call `c.get_finished()` on its children directly and did not
have `get_transfer_results` at all, so the test was correct when it was added in
#5148 (2026-09-17). vLLM 0.30.0 (2026-09-22) switched the aggregation over, and
since `requirements/common.txt` leaves vllm unpinned, CI picked it up the same
day and the matrix went red on every open PR.

The fix routes the mock's `get_transfer_results` through the real base
implementation, so the existing `get_finished` sequence stays the source of
truth and the test tracks whichever entry point `MultiConnector` uses.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

Test-only change, no production code touched. The file's 22 tests pass again and
the full CPU suite is green locally on CPython 3.13 (6246 passed, 280 skipped,
1 xpassed); before the change the same suite reported those 2 failures.

title: [fix][mp] hold server-side IPC events until their peer is done with them
body:
Refs #4419, #4640. Supersedes #5116.

**Both lifetimes are released on facts, not inference: the transfer stream itself drops an imported worker event once it has consumed the wait (a host callback queued right after it), and the worker itself releases an exported completion event once it is done querying it (`RELEASE_EVENT`).**

Before:

```
WORKER                            SERVER

ev_w ─────────────────────────→ import ev_w
                                queue wait(ev_w)
                                copy
                                create ev_s
                                record ev_s
ev_s handle ←────────────────── export ev_s
                                |
                                handler returns
                                |
                        ev_w dies TOO EARLY
                        ev_s dies TOO EARLY
```

After:

```
WORKER                            SERVER

ev_w ─────────────────────────→ ev_w' = import(ev_w)
                                registry.hold_imported(ev_w')
                                queue wait(ev_w')
                                queue host callback: drop ev_w'   <- fires only after the wait
                                copy
                                create ev_s
                                record ev_s
handle(ev_s) ←──────────────── export; registry.hold_exported(handle, ev_s)
                                |
                                handler returns: nothing dies
...
import(handle), query() == True   (adapter's get_finished)
RELEASE_EVENT(instance_id, handle) → drop ev_s
```

- **Exported events**: held in the worker's KV cache context's `IPCEventRegistry` until the engine adapter sends `RELEASE_EVENT(instance_id, handle)` once the transfer's future reports done (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and ATOM adapters, and the Q ring buffer). SGLang's async store hands its future to the SGLang-side connector, which must release the same way.
- **Imported events**: held by the context whose stream waits on them until the host callback queued on the transfer stream right after the wait fires.
- A cache context drops whatever it still holds when it is unregistered or reaped.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **High Risk**
> Changes ordering and lifetime of IPC events on the hot multiprocess transfer path; mistakes could reintroduce racey KV reads/writes or leak events until context teardown.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes premature teardown of cross-process GPU completion events, which could cause silent KV corruption under load when workers dropped handles before the server finished stream-ordered waits.
> 
> **Server:** Adds `IPCEventRegistry` on each cache context to pin **exported** completion events until the worker sends a new **`RELEASE_EVENT`** RPC, and **imported** worker events until a stream-ordered host callback runs immediately after `wait_event`. STORE/RETRIEVE/STORE_Q paths register holds on export/import; Q-store keeps exports on the worker’s KV context registry while imports live on the Q context.
> 
> **Workers:** vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, ATOM, and the Q ring adapter call `release_event` once store/retrieve futures complete (including shutdown drains where applicable). SGLang retrieve still treats event-free failures as server-owned lock cleanup.
> 
> **Wire/docs:** `RELEASE_EVENT` is added to the engine protocol, ZMQ client, and gRPC service; design doc documents the lifetime contract.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 72d1175f3dec86591df0871a4c4fbc8185d09f98. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>
<!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

title: feat: Direct PCIe BAR Memory Offloading and Multi-Region Virtual Allo…
body:
### Description
This PR introduces support for offloading KV cache directly to external PCIe BAR-backed IO memory (e.g., CXL memory expanders, NVMe Controller Memory Buffers, FPGA SRAM) without intermediate staging through host DRAM.

By mapping sysfs PCIe BAR resource files into user-space and registering them with CUDA using `cudaHostRegisterIoMemory`, GPU kernels obtain virtual addresses that resolve directly to BAR physical memory. This enables direct **peer-to-peer (P2P) transfers** and memory expansion while bypassing host DRAM bottlenecks.

Additionally, this change introduces a unified `VirtualMemoryAllocator` and resource manifest management system (`resource_manifest.py`) to manage heterogeneous memory tiers, multi-region allocation policies, and smart GPU topology bindings.
```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         LMCache Engine (L1)                           |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                   |
                       +-----------------------+
                       | VirtualMemoryAllocator|
                       +-----------------------+
                        /                     \
       +-----------------------+       +-----------------------+
       |   PCIe BAR Region 0   |       |      DRAM Region      |
       |  (/sys/.../resource4) |       |  (Pinned Host Memory) |
       +-----------------------+       +-----------------------+
```

---

#### 2. Memory Allocation Policies (`VirtualMemoryAllocator`)
The new `VirtualMemoryAllocator` abstracts heterogeneous memory regions (BAR and DRAM) into a unified memory pool. Memory distribution across these regions is governed by pluggable allocation policies:

* **Linear Policy (`LinearPolicy`)**:
  * Fills memory regions sequentially. Allocations are drawn from the primary region until full before spilling over to subsequent regions.
  * *Use Case*: Prioritizing high-bandwidth or low-latency tiers before falling back to secondary memory.
* **Capacity-Proportional Interleaving Policy (`InterleavingPolicy`)**:
  * Distributes allocations across active memory regions **proportionally to their total available capacity**.
  * Ensures uniform capacity saturation across heterogeneous memory tiers throughout runtime, rather than filling regions sequentially or ignoring capacity differences.
  * *Use Case*: Maximizing aggregate bandwidth across heterogeneous PCIe/CXL buses while maintaining balanced relative memory usage.
---

#### 3. GPU Resource Binding (`resource_manifest.py`)
The resource manifest allows specifying memory topographies and binding rules across GPU devices (e.g., `EqualCapacityBinding`, `InterleavedBinding`, `BandwidthWeightedBinding`).

> **Operational Constraint**: Smart resource allocation binding is supported **exclusively in Non-MP mode**. In Non-MP mode, a single central process manages all GPUs and receives the full resource allocation, whereas in Non-MP mode each GPU runs in a separate process with its own dedicated resources.
---

#### 4. Heterogeneous Memory Pool Support (PCIe BAR + DRAM)
The architecture is fully heterogeneous:
* Users are not limited to BAR-only regions; host **DRAM regions can be freely mixed alongside PCIe BAR regions** in the same configuration.
* The allocator handles backing store differences transparently, routing PyTorch tensors and CUDA calls appropriately according to region type.

---

#### 5. Known Limitations & Compatibility Matrix
* **L2 Cache Incompatibility**: This feature is designed specifically for **L1 direct offloading / local backends** and **cannot be run with L2 caching enabled**.
* **Non-MP Mode Requirement for Binding**: Resource binding features require single-process (non-MP) execution.
* **System Prerequisites**: Requires sysfs access permissions to PCIe BAR resource handles and proper IOMMU passthrough configuration (`intel_iommu=off` or passthrough).
---

#### 6. Key Changes Summary

* **C++/CUDA Driver Layer (`csrc/cuda/`)**:
  * `mem_alloc.cpp`: Implemented `alloc_pcie_bar_ptr` (`mmap` via `O_SYNC` + `cudaHostRegisterIoMemory`) and `free_pcie_bar_ptr`.
  * `mem_kernels.cu` & `transfer_plan_types.cuh`: Added asynchronous BAR D2D copy pipeline (`bar_memcpy_async`) and `is_bar` execution branch.
* **Memory Management (`lmcache/v1/memory_allocators/`)**:
  * Added `PcieBarMemoryAllocator` and unified `VirtualMemoryAllocator`.
  * Added pluggable allocation policies: `LinearPolicy` and `InterleavingPolicy`.
* **Manifest & Engine (`lmcache/v1/`)**:
  * Declarative YAML manifest describing available hardware resources (PCIe BAR devices and DRAM tiers) with capacity, path, and bandwidth metadata.
  * GPU device binding policies for multi-GPU setups: `EqualCapacityBinding `(contiguous slices), `InterleavedBinding `(round-robin slices from every device), `BandwidthWeightedBinding `(greedy bin-packing by bandwidth).
  * Supports inline config for non-MP mode (`extra_config.resource_manifest`), file reference, and environment variables (`PCIE_BAR_DEVICES`, `PCIE_BAR_DRAM_GB`, `PCIE_BAR_POLICY`).
---

#### 7. Integration with existing paths:

  * **Non-MP path**: `LocalCPUBackend.initialize_allocator` resolves the manifest and builds a `VirtualMemoryAllocator`.
  * **MP path**: `L1MemoryManager.create_memory_allocator` does the same via `_resolve_pcie_bar_allocator`.
  * `gpu_ops.py` detects BAR-backed objects via `_is_bar_backed()` and calls `bar_memcpy_async `for both H2D and D2H.
  * `build_staging_copies` sets `is_bar=True` on `StagingCopy `descriptors for BAR-backed objects, routing the MP batch transfer through the correct kernel path.
  * `--resource-manifest` CLI argument and `RESOURCE_MANIFEST `env var are added to the server argument parser.
  * Per-region token count logging added to store/retrieve paths in both `cache_engine.py` and `lmcache_driven_transfer.py`.

### Configuration Example

```
# resources.yaml
resources:
  - name: "bar_0"
    type: "pcie_bar"
    path: "/sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:41:00.0/resource4"
    capacity_gb: 64.0
  - name: "dram_tier"
    type: "dram"
    capacity_gb: 32.0
device_binding_policy: "equal_capacity"
allocation_policy: "interleaving"
```
Command line execution:
```
python -m lmcache.v1.server --resource-manifest /path/to/resources.yaml
```

title: [Bugfix] connector: publish batch tile results with acq_rel
body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Fixes #5296.

`ConnectorBase::handle_tile_completion` decremented `BatchState::remaining_tiles` with `memory_order_relaxed`. The tiles of a batch write disjoint slots of `per_key_results` and fill the caller's read buffers, then decrement; the tile that observes zero moves `per_key_results` into the completion. A relaxed RMW heads no release sequence, so there is no happens-before edge between a tile's writes and the last tile's read of them, nor between those writes and the consumer that later reads `result_bytes` through `drain_completions()`.

Decrementing with `acq_rel` gives each tile a release and the last tile an acquire. The relaxed `any_failed` accesses (`:608`, `:623`) are covered by the same edge, so they are left alone.

`handle_tile_completion` is private to `ConnectorBase`, so this applies to every derived connector — `fs`/`fs_native`, `redis`, `mooncake`, `nixl`, `aerospike`.

A regression test and a ThreadSanitizer CI job are included; see the reviewer notes.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

The regression guard is a ThreadSanitizer build, not a functional assertion. `csrc/storage_backends/tests/tsan_batch_completion.cpp` drives the FS connector through set / exists / get / delete with four workers and 64 keys, reading back every per-key result byte and every payload byte so the racing accesses are executed. Built without `-fsanitize=thread` it passes with or without the fix — on x86-64 TSO the defect does not change the result. Built instrumented:

```
unpatched tree:  exit 66, ThreadSanitizer: data race
this branch:     exit 0,  ok: 64 keys across set/exists/get/delete with 4 workers
```

`ConnectorBase` and the FS connector pull in no pybind and no torch, so `.github/workflows/native_tsan.yml` builds and runs it with a bare `g++` in well under a minute, gated on changes under `csrc/storage_backends/**`. `setarch -R` is there because ThreadSanitizer aborts with "unexpected memory mapping" on 6.x kernels.

If a separate workflow is not wanted, the job can fold into an existing one or be dropped — the test still runs by hand from the command in its header comment.

Locally clean with the pinned tool versions: `clang-format` 20.1.3, `codespell` 2.4.1, `actionlint` 1.7.7. I could not run the Python suite — this environment has no torch — so CI is the first full run.

title: feat(mp): add descriptor-driven per-chunk store completion events
body:
## Summary

This draft rebases the per-chunk store-completion work from #5272 onto the descriptor-driven RPC architecture in #5161.

The result intentionally has two commits:

1. `d21122f` - the complete #5161 descriptor-driven RPC refactor, squashed onto `dev`.
2. `2006bb8` - the per-chunk completion-event feature from #5272, adapted to that refactor.

Please review the second commit for the feature change.

## RPC architecture adaptation

`store_with_chunk_events` is declared once as a typed `@rpc_method` on `RequestClient`. That declaration yields the shared `RpcSpec` used by both transports.

The server implementation is a same-named `@request_handler(HandlerType.BLOCKING, requires_client_affinity=True)`; handler annotations are checked against the contract at server startup.

For gRPC, this PR adds `ChunkCompletion`, `StoreWithChunkEventsResponse`, and `StoreWithChunkEvents` to `LMCacheDrivenService`. Generated descriptors discover the method, map it to `store_with_chunk_events`, and compile the protobuf codecs.

No legacy `RequestType`, `ProtocolDefinition`, ZMQ client wrapper, or ZMQ server registration is added. New ZMQ operations are routed by their stable operation name and dynamically installed from `RpcSpec`.

## Feature behavior

The new store path returns the existing terminal completion event plus one source-safety completion event for each token chunk. The operation retains one reservation and one commit, while allowing callers to release source buffers chunk by chunk after D2H completion.

## Validation

- `uv run python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.transport.grpc_impl._proto_gen._generate`
- `uv run pytest -q tests/v1/multiprocess/test_protocols.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_grpc_transport.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_chunk_event_store.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_futures.py` - 67 passed, 13 skipped

title: [Fix] Bound device staging during first-rank KV retrieval
body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

With in-process MLA `save_only_first_rank`, retrieval currently creates a device copy of every cache-hit chunk before writing the serving engine's KV pages. The temporary device allocation therefore grows with the entire hit, even though the destination pages already exist. A large hit can exhaust device memory on either the source or a receiving rank.

Reserve a reusable payload buffer at engine initialization, shared by engines on the same device within a process. `retrieve_buffer_size` defaults to 64 MiB. Retrieval packs bounded windows, broadcasts them, writes the existing destination pages, and reuses the buffer after completion. Oversized chunks are sliced along the token dimension. Synchronous backend reads use bounded batches to preserve parallel disk I/O; asynchronous retrieval consumes existing prefetch results.

Ranks agree on admission and each window's readiness and completion using host collectives. A recoverable source, metadata, packing, or destination-write failure returns an all-false result on every rank. Source references remain owned until their reads finish; prefetched references are claimed once so later lookup cleanup cannot release them again. Failed device fences and communication errors propagate and disable the buffer. The engine retains its active source iterator until shutdown can fence the device.

The bounded transfer protocol, source ownership, and engine integration are kept together because buffer reuse depends on all three. The new transport is independent of vLLM; vLLM supplies a CPU-group agreement callback, and existing integrations can fall back to object broadcasts.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

This is a draft pending accelerator validation. Scope is non-layerwise, in-process first-rank retrieval. The budget covers the payload buffer, not final KV pages, connector workspaces, communication-library allocations, or the CPU cache. Separate processes have separate reservations. Integrations must initialize the engine before profiling memory for the final KV pool and invoke distributed retrievals in the same order. This does not introduce direct storage-to-page DMA or change the multiprocess protocol.

Validated locally on macOS with Python 3.12 and CPU-only native extensions, against `33962edb4f595ce4a0cbdd6a2bc5b59aeb05d0fa`:

- Relevant regression suite: **143 passed, 1 skipped, 72 deselected** using `-m 'not cuda'`. Includes real two-process Gloo admission/write/read/request-identity failures, successful subsequent requests, deferred-copy lifetimes, mixed-dtype alignment, bounded source batches, and source cleanup through the real cache engine.
- `SKIP=rust-fmt,rust-clippy pre-commit run --all-files`: passed. Rust is unchanged; these hooks were explicitly skipped on macOS.
- New transport and test modules also pass direct mypy checks.
- Sphinx HTML rendered and inspected. The strict full build reports **30 warnings**, identical to a clean build of the comparison revision; no warnings were added by this change. The full documentation build is therefore not clean on this baseline.
- Two CUDA memory-peak tests are included but were not executed locally. CUDA/NCCL and MLU/collective smoke tests, real serving-engine failure handling, and TTFT/throughput measurements remain to be run before marking this ready for review.

title: [Feature][CB] Per-engine-group scatter head size on CB_REGISTER_ROPE
body:
A model may size attention heads **per layer type** — Gemma-4 uses 256 on its sliding layers and 512 on its full-attention ones (`global_head_dim`) — so the single `head_size` carried by the rope registration has no correct value for it.

## Change

Adds an optional `group_head_size` to `CB_REGISTER_ROPE`. Empty (the default) preserves existing behaviour exactly: `head_size` covers every group. When present, `_CBRopeState.head_size_for_group()` resolves the group's own size for both consumers in the retrieve planner — `CBGroupSpec`'s scatter geometry and `_cb_group_rope_geometry`.

Backward compatible: every uniform-head model registers an empty list and takes the unchanged legacy path.

title: Refactor multiprocess RPC contract discovery
body:
## Background

Multiprocess RPC metadata was previously duplicated across `RequestType`, `ProtocolDefinition`, `RequestClient`, ZMQ client/server glue, the gRPC codec registry, protobuf services, and business handlers. Adding one ordinary RPC that supports both ZMQ and gRPC required keeping several registries and adapters synchronized; a missed edit could surface only at runtime.

This PR consolidates the RPC contract into one discoverable Python API: fully typed `RequestClient` methods marked with `@rpc_method`. `RequestClient` is the **declaration site for the contract**, not a server dependency or a client instance that the server must construct. `rpc.py` derives an immutable `RpcSpec` (operation name, parameters, and response type) from that API, and both ZMQ and gRPC consume the same specs.

## How the new mechanism works

1. Declare an `@rpc_method` on `RequestClient`. Its method name is the stable operation name, while its parameters and `MessagingFuture[T]` annotation are the payload and response contract.
2. `rpc.py` reflects those methods into `RpcSpec` objects. The ZMQ client is driven by those specs and sends requests by operation; a server-side `@request_handler` binds to the same operation by method name, leaving the decorator responsible only for scheduling and affinity.
3. gRPC iterates generated protobuf descriptors, finds the same-named `RpcSpec`, and uses it to build codecs and validate handler types. New services are discovered from descriptors too; there is no hand-maintained gRPC service registry.
4. ZMQ operation ids `1..33` retain their existing wire representation for deployed-peer compatibility. New operations use their string names on the wire. The compatibility boundary is therefore explicit: existing operations keep their ids, and new operations do not consume a global integer id.

## Change-surface comparison

The file counts below are the manually maintained touch points for one **ordinary RPC exposed through both ZMQ and gRPC**. Generated protobuf Python bindings are not counted as manual edits.

| Scenario | Previous manual changes | New manual changes | What no longer changes, and why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Add an ordinary RPC | **7 files**: `RequestType` in `protocols/base.py`, a `ProtocolDefinition` in `protocols/*.py`, the method in `transport/base.py`, a ZMQ client wrapper, a ZMQ server handler spec, the relevant `.proto`, and the business-module handler | **3 files**: the `@rpc_method` in `transport/base.py`, the request/response/service method in the relevant `.proto`, and a same-named `@request_handler` in the business module | No manual `RequestType`, `ProtocolDefinition`, ZMQ client wrapper, or ZMQ server handler spec. `RpcSpec` is discovered from the typed method, both ZMQ endpoints consume it, and the handler is discovered by name. |
| Add a Python business type that is not exposed as an RPC | **1 type-definition file**, plus the business code that uses it | **The same** | This is not an RPC extension, so the PR does not manufacture a benefit. When the type becomes an RPC parameter or response, it participates in the 7-to-3 reduction above. |
| Add a gRPC message | **1 `.proto` source file**; generated bindings update automatically. If it belongs to a new RPC, the 7 touch points above also apply | **The same `.proto` edit**; generated bindings update automatically. If it belongs to a new RPC, add `RequestClient` and the handler for 3 total touch points | The protobuf schema remains the cross-language wire contract and should not be replaced by Python reflection. The duplicated protocol and ZMQ registration work disappears. |
| Add a gRPC service | Add or edit the service `.proto`, then repeat the **7** touch points for every RPC in it | Add or edit the service `.proto`; each RPC needs only the **3** touch points above | No manual gRPC service registry. Generated descriptors enumerate the new service and methods, then resolve the contract by name. |

This does **not** mean a new RPC never needs transport awareness. Its author must still write protobuf to define the gRPC wire schema and ensure that its types can be represented by the ZMQ and gRPC codecs. The refactor removes the coupling that required every extension to manually synchronize the ZMQ operation enum, protocol definition, client wrapper, and server handler mapping.

## Compatibility and constraints

- `RequestClient` is the current Python contract source of truth; the server imports derived metadata, not a client instance.
- The legacy ZMQ id mapping is frozen and covered by tests. Do not add new RPCs to the legacy integer table.
- The operation name, `RequestClient` method, protobuf method, and handler method must correspond. Descriptor and annotation validation fails early when they do not.
- Protobuf messages still follow normal compatibility rules: never reuse field numbers and evolve schemas append-only. This PR does not bypass protobuf schema-evolution responsibilities.

## Validation

- `NO_GPU_EXT=1 uv pip install -e .`
- `uv run pytest tests/v1/multiprocess/test_protocols.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_client.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_mq.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_grpc_transport.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_p2p_controller.py tests/v1/multiprocess/test_autostart_health.py -q`: 109 passed, 1 skipped
- `SKIP=rust-fmt,rust-clippy uvx pre-commit run --all-files`

title: [Fix][MP] Evict L1 residents on prefetch allocation failure
body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

An L2 cache hit can fall back to recomputation when its restore buffers do not fit in L1, even while L1 is below the background eviction watermark. For example, 18 resident chunks in a 28-chunk pool leave room for only 10 chunks: an 11-chunk L2 restore fails at 64% utilization, so the 80% watermark never triggers eviction.

Enable demand eviction for L2 prefetch reservations. After allocation fails, select candidates using the configured L1 eviction policy, reclaim enough aligned bytes to cover the deficit, and retry allocation once. The regression now restores all 11 chunks after evicting one resident, and checks the loaded tensor contents.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

- Candidate selection, eligibility checks, deletion, and the allocation retry run under the L1 manager lock. A concurrent store cannot consume the reclaimed space before the retry. Read-locked residents, staging writers, and keys in the reservation are protected.
- Preflight the available victim bytes before deleting anything. Oversized reservations or insufficient reclaimable bytes return OOM without evicting residents. The existing listener/event path reports actual deletions, keeping the policy's candidate list consistent.
- The recovery path is enabled for L2 prefetch through `StorageManager`; direct write reservations retain their existing default. Candidate selection honors `noop` and per-salt isolated policies.
- Recovery is per object-group reservation. Buffers reserved for earlier groups stay write-locked; an unsuccessful load releases them through the existing cleanup path. This is not a transaction across all groups.
- Byte capacity does not guarantee contiguous space. Fragmentation without a byte deficit skips demand eviction; a retry that still fails stops after that single eviction pass. Candidate collection scans the policy's pool under the L1 lock, so large-pool latency and real serving TTFT remain to be measured.

**Validation**:

On macOS arm64, Python 3.12.13 and PyTorch 2.13.0, using the real common native extension built with `NO_GPU_EXT=1`:

- Focused L1, prefetch, eviction-policy, GDS address-allocation, and capacity suites: **264 passed, 2 skipped**. The two accelerator-gated modules were `test_l1_memory_manager.py` and `test_distributed_storage_manager.py`.

title: [Feat] report hidden-state coverage through the lookup path
body:
<!--  Thanks for your contribution to LMCache!  Here are some tips for you:
1. Make sure to read the Contributing Guide before submitting your PR: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md
2. If this PR closes another issue, add 'Fixes #<issue number>' somewhere in the PR summary. GitHub will automatically close that issue when this PR gets merged. Alternatively, adding 'Refs #<issue number>' will not close the issue, but help provide the reviewer more context.-->

## Problem

`get_num_new_matched_tokens()` is where vLLM decides how much prefill to skip, and it only ever learns how many tokens LMCache holds KV for. Hidden states live in a separate pool with its own capacity, its own LRU and its own per-layer contents, so the two quantities drift: the pools evict independently, and the shipped defaults size hidden states at `max_hidden_state_cpu_size=2.0` against `max_local_cpu_size=5.0`, so hidden states go first while their KV survives. A store is also per layer, so a caller that needs hidden states from more than one layer loses the whole prefix when any one of them is missing.

When KV covers more than hidden states do, the engine skips a prefill whose hidden states nobody can supply. Nothing detects that at schedule time — the consumer only finds out in the worker, after the KV is committed and the recompute it would have needed is gone.

Not hypothetical for consumers that condition a downstream stage on hidden states. In vLLM-Omni the talker stage is conditioned on the thinker's hidden states, and a short restore leaves it with a truncated prefix; the audio degrades with no error anywhere. The two tiers there also align on different multiples — vLLM's prefix cache reports block multiples (16) while LMCache's coverage is chunk-aligned (256) — so agreeing is the coincidence, not the rule.

## Approach

Report hidden-state coverage alongside the KV hit length, so a caller can commit to `min(KV, HS)` instead of to KV alone.

`request_configs` already travels end to end and is free-form, so the request side needs no format change: a caller names the layers it cares about under `lmcache.hidden_state_layer_idxs`. When that key is present the lookup server appends a second 4-byte field to its reply.

That keeps both directions working. A new client against an old server gets its key ignored and a 4-byte reply, reports coverage as unknown, and the caller falls back to the KV count. An old client against a new server never sends the key, so the reply is unchanged.

Four small additions:

- `HiddenStateStore.coverage(chunks, layer_idxs)` walks the request's `(start, end, key)` chunks and stops at the first gap, so the result is a prefix length directly comparable with what `lookup` reports for KV.
- `LMCacheEngine.lookup_hidden_states(...)` uses the same chunking and prefix semantics as `lookup`, and returns 0 when no hidden-state store is configured.
- `LookupClientInterface.lookup_hidden_state_coverage(lookup_id)` defaults to `None`, meaning "cannot answer". `LMCacheLookupClient` fills it in when the server reported it.
- The other clients that can answer do. `LMCacheBypassLookupClient` holds the engine, so it queries it directly. `HitLimitLookupClient` and `ChunkStatisticsLookupClient` wrap an inner client and forward to it. Leaving any of them on the default would have made coverage unreadable under a supported configuration, which is the silent degradation this query exists to prevent. `LMCacheAsyncLookupClient` and `MooncakeLookupClient` keep the default: the first speaks its own protocol to a separate server and would need that extended too, and the second fronts an external store with no hidden-state pool.

## Tests

`tests/v1/test_hidden_state_store.py` covers the coverage walk: full prefix covered, a gap partway through truncates to the prefix before it, every requested layer is required, and an empty store reports 0.

`tests/v1/lookup_client/test_lookup_hidden_state_coverage.py` covers the wire: a 4-byte reply leaves coverage unknown rather than reading as zero, an 8-byte one carries it, coverage takes the minimum across ranks the way the KV count does, the request rides in `request_configs` so the frame layout is unchanged, and clearing a lookup drops both fields. Two more cover the bypass client answering from its engine and leaving the engine alone when the caller did not ask.

The server-side branch that appends the field is a two-line conditional inside `LMCacheLookupServer.__init__`'s closure; I checked that by reading rather than by test, since making it callable would mean restructuring for testability.

title: [Perf] Reduce bringup time with parallel and batched recovery slot-header validation
body:
<!--  Thanks for your contribution to LMCache!  Here are some tips for you:
1. Make sure to read the Contributing Guide before submitting your PR: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md
2. If this PR closes another issue, add 'Fixes #<issue number>' somewhere in the PR summary. GitHub will automatically close that issue when this PR gets merged. Alternatively, adding 'Refs #<issue number>' will not close the issue, but help provide the reviewer more context.-->


**What this PR does / why we need it**

This PR addresses #3753 by reducing RawBlockCore restart recovery time through engine-specific optimizations: multithreaded slot-header validation for the POSIX I/O engine and batched reads for the io_uring I/O engine.

During restart, recovery validates checkpoint entries against on-device slot headers. For multi-terabyte raw-block caches, this can require hundreds of thousands or millions of small reads, making serial validation a major contributor to bringup time.

*Recovery benchmark*

Performance was measured with a local synthetic recovery harness that writes checkpoint metadata and slot headers without full payloads.
The benchmark ran on a Samsung BM1743 NVMe SSD using an 8 TiB cache with 16 MiB slots, corresponding to approximately 524K recovered entries.

```bash
python benchmarks/storage_backend_io/raw_block_recovery_bringup_bench.py \
  --device-path /dev/nvmeXn1 --cache-space-gb 8192 --slot-bytes 16777216 \
  --measure --io-engine posix io_uring --threads 1 8 --repeats 5
```

| recovery path | median | speedup vs serial |
|---|---|---|
| `posix` serial (threads=1) | 70.59s | 1.00× |
| `posix` threadpool (threads=8) | 16.31s | 4.33× |
| **`io_uring` batched** | **11.55s** | **6.11×** |

Both optimizations substantially reduce recovery time: the 8-thread POSIX path improves over serial validation, while batched `io_uring` provides an additional ~1.4× speedup and reaches 6.11× over serial.


**Special notes for reviewers**

* `use_uring_cmd` (NVMe passthrough) batching is excluded because it requires separate low-level validation.
* If a batch read fails, recovery falls back to per-slot reads to identify the failed entries.

title: [MP][Coordinator] Add Kafka cache-event source
body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Adds the coordinator side of the Kafka cache-event transport: `KafkaCacheEventSource` consumes the topic `KafkaCacheEventSink` (#5285) publishes to and feeds `EventGate`, so events published to Kafka reach the key directory, usage view, and eviction controller through the same gate as `POST /events`.

- Exactly one source per coordinator, selected by `--event-transport {http,kafka}` (default `http`). Under `kafka`, `POST /events` answers 404. One ordered path per emitter stream is what the gate's per-emitter `seq` cursor assumes.
- One poll thread; each record is a `CacheEventsRequest` JSON envelope (the `POST /events` body) keyed by `instance_id`, and its batches go to `EventGate.ingest_batches`, so a partition (one instance's stream) is admitted in order.
- At-least-once: an offset is stored only after the gate has seen the record and is committed by the consumer group, so a restart resumes where the last coordinator stopped; the gate's dedup absorbs redelivery. Undecodable records and consumer exceptions are logged and skipped.
- `--kafka-bootstrap-servers` (required under `kafka`), `--kafka-topic`, `--kafka-group-id`. `confluent-kafka` ships as the optional `lmcache[kafka]` extra and is imported only when the source is built.
- Fake `confluent_kafka` consumer for tests, including an end-to-end `create_app` test that reads a record into the key directory and sees `POST /events` closed.

Refs #4226.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

- Follows #5285 (the MP-server producer, merged): reuses its `lmcache[kafka]` extra, topic default, and `fake_kafka.py` test double (extended with a consumer).
- Replay is operator-driven for now (reset the consumer group's offsets). A coordinator-driven seek on `gap_detected` is the follow-up noted in `ingest.md`.

title: [Bugfix] Keep lookup pin ownership out of synchronous retrieve cleanup
body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

Blocking gets acquire references, not ownership of lookup pins. Active synchronous `retrieve()` currently consumes a lookup pin anyway, and the subsequent `lookup_unpin()` consumes it again. Pins carry no per-request ownership, so for a shared chunk one request can silently release another request's pin without a negative-count warning.

Keep lookup pins owned by `lookup_unpin()`. In the synchronous non-layerwise vLLM load path, release each request's lookup ledger immediately after retrieval, before the next request may need CPU staging space. The existing async, passive-rank, and PD cleanup branches are preserved.

Removing that compensating unpin exposes an older asymmetry that predates this PR: the two `LocalCPUBackend` clear paths treat pins differently.

| Path | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `clear(tokens=None)` | skips pinned objects via `can_evict` |
| `clear(tokens=[...])` → `remove(key, force=True)` | popped the key without looking at `pin_count` |

Because the lookup ledger tracks *keys*, once a targeted clear pops the key the later `unpin(key)` finds nothing and the pin is stranded until the pin monitor times out, holding CPU capacity. The old `retrieve()` unpin happened to mask this for the single-pin case; it did not fix it, and it could not fix the shared-chunk case.

So `remove()` now releases the pins of the entry it abandons, but only on the forced path. `force=False` is the internal eviction path, where `can_evict` (`not is_pinned and ref_count == 1`) already filters pinned objects out; a pinned object arriving there means the caller is confused, so the pin is preserved rather than silently dropped. The loop releases the full count because *every* holder's `lookup_unpin` will be a no-op once the key is gone.

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

- The invalidation semantics of `clear(tokens=...)` do not change. Dirty KV is still really deleted; it just no longer leaks capacity.
- `LocalDiskBackend.remove()` was checked and deliberately left alone. It pops `DiskCacheMetadata` and `os.remove()`s the file; the pin lives on the discarded metadata and no allocator capacity is held, so there is no equivalent leak.
- The `lookup_pins` ledger structure is unchanged. Storing memory objects instead of keys would also require changing the `batched_get(keys=...)` call sites in `cache_engine.py` and the block-mapping reuse path; that is a larger refactor and is out of scope here.
- Every object-level `unpin()` in `cache_engine.py` is already guarded by `if memory_obj.is_pinned`, so a pin released early by forced removal cannot cause an over-release at those sites.

**Validation** (CPU only, Python 3.10, editable install):

- `tests/v1/test_retrieve_pin_ownership.py`: **20 passed, 0 xfail**. The targeted-clear case is red before the backend fix (`--runxfail` → 1 failed) and green after it.
- `tests/v1/storage_backend/test_local_cpu_backend.py`: **30 passed**.
- `tests/v1/internal_api_server/test_cache_clear.py`: **6 passed** — existing clear behavior unchanged.
- `tests/v1/test_vllm_sync_load_pin_cleanup.py`: **5 passed** using local vLLM import/type stubs; the LMCache adapter/engine logic is real. These check ordering and eviction eligibility, not real disk pressure or vLLM/GPU integration.
- `tests/v1/test_cache_engine.py`: **68 skipped** — every case there is CUDA-gated and this environment is CPU only, so that suite is untested here rather than passing.
- Changed-file Ruff lint/format, isort, codespell, and `git diff --check` pass. mypy on the new tests with `--follow-imports=skip` passes; a normal mypy run on the changed files still times out after 90 seconds, so full type checking was not completed locally.
- Full pre-commit, the full suite, and GPU tests were not run. OpenTelemetry deprecation warnings remain. This is not a general async/layerwise pin-lifecycle fix.

title: [Bugfix][MP] Limit cache stores to prompt chunks by default
body:
**What this PR does / why we need it**:

The MP connector currently stores a new chunk when decode tokens complete the
partial chunk at the end of a prompt. Because the chunk includes sampled output,
its hash can change on every request, so a fixed prompt workload continues to
write new cache entries after the prompt cache is warm.

This caps MP stores at the request's prompt length by default. Decode caching
can still be enabled explicitly with:

```json
"lmcache.mp.save_decode_cache": true
```

Fixes #5230

**Special notes for your reviewers**:

On a running MP server (chunk_size=256, prompt=290): OSL 100 stored 256 tokens;
OSL 250 hit the prefix and did not store an extra [256, 512) chunk.

OSL 100:

```text
prompt_tokens=290 max_tokens=100
Final connector metadata: direction=STORE, num_blocks=4
Stored 256 tokens in 0.287 seconds
```

OSL 250:

```text
prompt_tokens=290 max_tokens=250
vLLM hit is: 256, Need to load is 0
(no additional Stored line)
```

MP connector regression tests cover the default prompt-only behavior, the
decode-cache opt-in, immediate and lazy stores, prompt/decode chunk boundaries,
preemption, and the existing per-request store limit.
